summary: Extends BGP-4 so it can carry routing information for network protocols other than IPv4, such as IPv6 and VPN address families. The extensions are backward compatible, so upgraded routers still interoperate with older ones.

eli5.summary: BGP is how big networks tell each other which roads exist. This lets the same messages describe roads for many kinds of addresses, not just the old kind, while old routers still understand the rest.

questions: how does bgp carry ipv6 routes
subtitle: How BGP-4 learned to carry routes for IPv6, VPNs and other address types without breaking old routers.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 only knew how to describe IPv4 routes. Three pieces of its data, the NEXT_HOP attribute, AGGREGATOR and NLRI, were tied to IPv4 addresses.
tldr.mechanism: Two new optional, non-transitive attributes, MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI, carry an address family, a next hop and the routes themselves. Speakers agree to use them through capability advertisement.
tldr.outcome: A router with the extensions can still talk to one without them, because the old router simply ignores the new attributes. This RFC replaces RFC 2858 and was later updated by RFC 7606.

today: RFC 4760 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2858 and is updated by RFC 7606. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why BGP-4 Needed Extending
sections.content:
The base BGP-4 protocol (RFC 4271) carries only three pieces of information that are specific to IPv4: the NEXT_HOP attribute, the AGGREGATOR attribute and the NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information), which is written as IPv4 address prefixes.

The RFC assumes every BGP speaker has an IPv4 address anyway, which is still used in AGGREGATOR. So only two things have to be added: a way to tie a particular Network Layer protocol to the next hop information, and a way to tie it to the NLRI. The protocol is identified by a pair of an Address Family (from the IANA registry) and a Subsequent Address Family.

The RFC also observes that next hop information only matters when announcing reachable destinations, not when withdrawing them. That is why reachable and unreachable destinations get separate attributes.
sections.eli5: Imagine a road map that can only list streets with one kind of house number. This change adds a label saying which kind of numbering each list uses.

sections.title: The Two New Attributes
sections.content:
MP_REACH_NLRI (Type Code 14) advertises feasible routes and the next hop to use for them. It holds an Address Family Identifier (2 octets), a Subsequent Address Family Identifier (1 octet), the length of the next hop address (1 octet), the next hop network address (variable), a reserved octet and the NLRI (variable). The reserved octet MUST be set to 0 and SHOULD be ignored on receipt.

MP_UNREACH_NLRI (Type Code 15) withdraws routes. It holds only the two identifiers and the withdrawn routes. An UPDATE that contains it is not required to carry any other path attributes.

Both attributes are optional and non-transitive. A speaker without multiprotocol support ignores them and does not pass them on, which is what makes the change backward compatible.

An UPDATE carrying MP_REACH_NLRI MUST also carry ORIGIN and AS_PATH, and in IBGP it MUST also carry LOCAL_PREF. If the only NLRI is the one in MP_REACH_NLRI, the message SHOULD NOT carry NEXT_HOP, and a receiver SHOULD ignore it if present. An UPDATE SHOULD NOT list the same prefix of the same AFI and SAFI in more than one of the withdrawn routes, reachability, MP_REACH_NLRI or MP_UNREACH_NLRI fields, because the processing of such a message is undefined.
sections.eli5: One new note says 'here are roads you can use, and go through this town next'. The other says 'these roads are closed'. Routers that do not know the notes just ignore them.

sections.title: How Routes Are Written
sections.content:
Each NLRI entry is a pair of a one-octet Length and a variable-length Prefix. Length is the size of the address prefix in bits. A length of zero means a prefix that matches all addresses of the address family, and the prefix itself then takes zero octets.

The Prefix field holds the prefix bits followed by enough trailing bits to end on an octet boundary. The value of those trailing bits is irrelevant.
sections.eli5: Each route is written as how many digits matter, then those digits, padded out so everything lines up. The padding does not mean anything.

sections.title: Subsequent Address Family Values
sections.content:
This RFC defines two values for the Subsequent Address Family Identifier (SAFI): 1 for NLRI used for unicast forwarding and 2 for NLRI used for multicast forwarding. An implementation MAY support all, some or none of them.

For the registry, IANA registers and maintains SAFI values. Values 5 through 63 are assigned by Standards Action or Early IANA Allocation, and 67 through 127 are first come first served. Values 0 and 255 are reserved, and 241 through 254 are for private use. SAFI 3 is reserved and deprecated: RFC 2858 assigned it for a use that was never fully implemented.
sections.eli5: A second label says what the list is for. For now there are two: roads for ordinary trips and roads for sending to many people at once.

sections.title: When an Attribute Is Wrong
sections.content:
If a speaker decides that a received MP_REACH_NLRI or MP_UNREACH_NLRI attribute is incorrect, it MUST delete all BGP routes it received from that neighbor with the same AFI and SAFI. For the rest of that session it SHOULD ignore all later routes with that AFI and SAFI.

The speaker MAY also terminate the session. If it does, it SHOULD send a Notification with the code and subcode for UPDATE Message Error and Optional Attribute Error.
sections.eli5: If a router gets a garbled road list for one kind of address, it throws out everything it learned about that kind from that neighbor and may stop talking to them.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use the Extensions
sections.content:
A speaker that uses the extensions SHOULD use the Capability Advertisement procedures (RFC 3392) to find out whether it can use them with a given peer. The Capability Code is 1, the Capability Length is 4, and the Capability Value is the AFI (16 bits), a reserved octet and the SAFI (8 bits). The reserved octet SHOULD be set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

A speaker supporting several AFI and SAFI pairs sends several capabilities. For routing information to flow in both directions for one pair, each speaker MUST advertise that pair to the other.
sections.eli5: Before swapping lists, each router says which kinds of addresses it can handle. They only swap lists for kinds both of them announced.

sections.title: Differences from Earlier Specifications
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 2858, this document makes the next hop consistent with the NEXT_HOP attribute, removes and deprecates SAFI 3, and changes how the SAFI space is partitioned: unused values 130, 131, 135 through 139 and 141 through 240 are reserved. It also renames the Number of SNPAs field to Reserved and removes the other SNPA information.

Compared with RFC 2283, it limits each MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attribute to a single instance of its tuple. It clarifies handling of an UPDATE with no other NLRI, clarifies error handling, specifies the use of capability advertisement and adds an IANA Considerations section.
sections.eli5: This version tidies up the older one: it drops an idea nobody finished, makes some parts consistent, and says exactly how to handle mistakes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is one sentence: the extension does not change the underlying security issues inherent in the existing BGP.
sections.eli5: This change does not make BGP safer or less safe. Whatever risks it had before, it still has.
